prompt: Which statement is consistent with the doctrinal armor mission?
options: Armor performs reconnaissance and surveillance and provides security for the unit to which it is attached
Armor closes with and neutralizes enemy forces by fire, maneuver and shock effect in coordination with other arms
Armor closes with the enemy to destroy or capture him or repel his assault by close combat and counterattack
Armor conducts ISO activities in peacetime only when it is attached to an infantry unit
explanation: Page 14 gives the armor mission as closing with and neutralizing enemy forces by fire, maneuver and shock effect in coordination with other arms, with ISO also allowed. The second and third options are the cavalry (page 16) and mechanized infantry (page 18) missions.

prompt: Which units match, in order, these missions: (1) reconnaissance, surveillance and security; (2) neutralize the enemy by fire, maneuver and shock effect; (3) close with the enemy to destroy or capture him?
options: Tank, cavalry, mechanized infantry
Mechanized infantry, tank, cavalry
Cavalry, tank, mechanized infantry
Cavalry, mechanized infantry, tank
explanation: Pages 16 to 18 give these three missions to cavalry, tank and mechanized infantry, in that order.

prompt: The armor mission is to neutralize enemy forces by fire, maneuver and shock effect:
options: Independently of other arms
After other arms have closed with the enemy
In coordination with other arms
Only in a peacetime environment
explanation: Page 14 says armor neutralizes the enemy by fire, maneuver and shock effect in coordination with other arms; page 13 adds that fire and maneuver are combined and controlled.

prompt: During an exercise, crews survive small arms fire, the radio net fails during maneuver and the vehicles keep pace over varied terrain. Which characteristic of armor was degraded?
options: Armor protection
Intensive and flexible communication
Mobility
Flexibility
explanation: Page 20 lists armor protection, mobility and intensive and flexible communication as characteristics. Only communication, the radio net, failed in the scenario.

prompt: Which characteristics, in order, are shown by these features: the 25 mm cannon, the amphibious M113A2 hull, and Level 4 ballistic protection on the Sabrah?
options: Mobility, firepower, armor protection
Armor protection, mobility, firepower
Firepower, armor protection, mobility
Firepower, mobility, armor protection
explanation: Page 20 lists the characteristics; the 25 mm cannon (page 75) is firepower, the amphibious hull (page 73) is mobility and Level 4 protection (page 82) is armor protection.

prompt: During a dismount, who is responsible for both the maneuver of the dismount team and the positioning of the AV?
options: The carrier team leader
The driver
The squad leader or platoon leader
The company first sergeant
explanation: Page 31 says the SL or PL is responsible for both the maneuver of the dismount team and the positioning of the AV. The first sergeant appears only as a possible resource manager in planning (page 69).

prompt: Each squad in the lesson's chart has 9 enlisted, of whom the three-man carrier team stays with the AIFV. How many squad members dismount in all nine squads of a mechanized infantry company?
explanation: Page 26 gives three squads of 9 per platoon and page 25 three platoons per company, or nine squads. Page 27 puts three in the carrier team, so six per squad dismount: 9 x 6 = 54.

prompt: Which allocation fits these tasks, in order: assault unprepared, suppressed defenses; infiltrate enemy positions; fix the enemy to allow maneuver?
options: Mounted, mounted, dismounted
Mounted, dismounted, dismounted
Dismounted, mounted, mounted
Dismounted, dismounted, dismounted
explanation: Page 28 lists assaulting unprepared, suppressed defenses as a mounted capability. Page 29 lists infiltrating enemy positions and fixing the enemy to allow maneuver as dismounted capabilities.

prompt: Which statement about the employment of mechanized infantry is correct?
options: It cannot be used against tank units, and AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks
It can be used against tank units if it dismounts to fix the enemy
It can lead an assault against tank units because AIFVs can maneuver with tanks
It lacks the firepower to support tanks and is kept out of every armored attack
explanation: Page 69 says mechanized infantry cannot be used against tank units, and page 30 says AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks. Page 28 lets it maneuver with tanks, which is not the same as fighting tank units.

prompt: Eight soldiers dismounted in order 1 to 8. As they remount, the enemy fires from the right. Which drill applies, and who boards first?
options: Mount from the right (under fire from left); soldier 8
Mount from the left (under fire from right); soldier 1
Mount from the left (under fire from right); soldier 8
Mount from the right (under fire from left); soldier 1
explanation: Page 50 shows mount from the left (under fire from the right). Page 31 says the first to dismount is the last to mount, so soldier 8 boards first, one at a time with cover provided (page 45).

prompt: Which list gives all the mounting procedures in the lesson?
options: Mount; mount from the right; mount from the left
Mount from the right; mount from the left; mount from the right (under fire from left); mount from the left (under fire from right)
Mount; mount from the right; mount from the left; mount from the right (under fire from left); mount from the left (under fire from left)
Mount; mount from the right; mount from the left; mount from the right (under fire from left); mount from the left (under fire from right)
explanation: Pages 46 to 50 give five mounting procedures: mount, mount from the right, mount from the left, mount from the right (under fire from left) and mount from the left (under fire from right).

prompt: Which list contains the fundamentals of cavalry in the lesson?
options: Commander's eyes and ears; main attack; spread of combat power along the whole front
Rear security; economy of force; resupply of the main body
Commander's eyes and ears; economy of force; concentration of combat power at the decisive place and time
Reserve; counterattack; concentration of combat power at the decisive place and time
explanation: Pages 53 and 54 describe cavalry as the commander's eyes and ears, an economy of force, and a means to concentrate combat power at the decisive time and point.

prompt: A separate cavalry troop with a light brigade covers a flank through dense forest and a major river. Which statement fits the lesson?
options: It is a heavy unit working for the division commander, and the terrain does not restrict its mobility
It is a light unit working for the brigade commander, limited by high logistics needs and restricted mobility
It is a heavy unit because separate troops are always heavy, whatever the brigade type
It is a light unit working for the division commander, and its logistics requirements are low
explanation: Page 58 says the separate troop is heavy or light according to its brigade and operates for the brigade commander; page 61 lists high logistics requirements and terrain-restricted mobility.

prompt: A tank platoon attached to an infantry battalion will fight enemy armor at night, possibly on an NBC battlefield, for several days. Which plan matches the lesson?
options: Anti-tank fires, thermal sights at night, avoid an NBC battlefield, support from FFSU and division CSS
Anti-tank fires, thermal sights at night, operate under NBC, support from FFSU and division CSS
Anti-tank fires, fight by day only, operate under NBC, Classes III, V and IX from infantry trucks
Direct fire against infantry only, thermal sights at night, operate under NBC, support from FFSU and division CSS
explanation: Page 66 gives tanks anti-tank fires, thermal sights for night fighting and operation on a conventional or NBC battlefield. Page 68 says they rely on the FFSU and division CSS because infantry units lack the transport for Classes III, V and IX.

prompt: Which of the following lists limitations of tanks?
options: Dependent on flatbeds for deployment; high logistics requirements; mobility restricted by dense forest
Lacks main battle tank protection; vulnerable to anti-armor weapons and mines; mobility and firepower restricted in extremely close terrain
Vulnerable to small arms fire; needs sufficient time to mount and dismount; restricted to certain avenues of approach
Cannot use thermal sights at night; limited to a conventional battlefield; dependent on flatbeds for deployment
explanation: Pages 67 and 68 list the light tank's lack of main battle tank protection, its vulnerability to anti-armor weapons and antitank mines, and restricted mobility and firepower in extremely close terrain. The other lists mix in cavalry or mechanized infantry items or deny tank capabilities.

prompt: A mechanized infantry planning checklist has where to dismount troops, objective to combat trains distance, Ex-O or First Sergeant as resource manager, and no use against tank units. Which two items are missing?
options: Surface danger zone; SBF positions
Indirect fire weapon support; distance from main body
Security operations; cover against enemy air
Weapon range; avenue of approach restrictions
explanation: Page 69 lists six mechanized infantry considerations, including weapon range and avenue of approach restrictions. The other pairs come from the cavalry (page 70) and tank (page 71) lists.

prompt: Which units match, in order, these planning considerations: (1) Ex-O as resource manager; (2) indirect fire weapon support; (3) surface danger zone?
options: Cavalry, tank, mechanized infantry
Tank, mechanized infantry, cavalry
Mechanized infantry, cavalry, tank
Mechanized infantry, tank, cavalry
explanation: Pages 69 to 71 list the Ex-O or First Sergeant as resource manager for mechanized infantry, indirect fire weapon support for cavalry and surface danger zone for tanks.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which statement about the M113A2, Commando V-150S and Simba data sheets is correct?
options: The M113A2 has the shortest road range (482.80 km); the Simba is the fastest (100 kph)
The V-150S has the shortest road range (644 km); the Simba is the fastest (100 kph)
The M113A2 has the shortest road range (482.80 km); the M113A2 is the fastest (66 kph)
The Simba has the shortest road range (660 km); the V-150S is the fastest (100 kph)
explanation: Page 75 gives the M113A2 a 482.80 km range and 66 kph; page 81 gives the V-150S 644 km; page 82 gives the Simba 660 km and 100 kph.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which data are common to the 25 mm cannons of the AIFV and the M113A2 IFV with the Unmanned Turret System?
options: HE 1,325 m/s, AP 1,100 m/s, 3,000 m maximum effective range
HE 1,100 m/s, AP 1,325 m/s, 3,000 m maximum effective range
HE 1,100 m/s, AP 1,325 m/s, 6,800 m maximum effective range
HE 1,100 m/s, AP 1,325 m/s, 1,700 m maximum effective range
explanation: Pages 75 and 76 give both 25 mm cannons HE 1,100 m/s, AP 1,325 m/s and a 3,000 m maximum effective range. 6,800 m is a maximum range and 1,700 m is the RCWS (page 74).

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which engine and fuel capacity are common to the M113A2 APC (Ambulance), the Mounted Mortar System and the Fire Support Vehicle?
options: 260 hp Detroit Diesel 6V53T; 360 L
212 hp Detroit Diesel 6V53; 360 L
212 hp Detroit Diesel 6V53; 300 L
260 hp Detroit Diesel 6V53T; 300 L
explanation: Pages 77, 78 and 81 give these variants the M113A2's 212 hp Detroit Diesel 6V53 and 360 L of fuel (page 73). The 260 hp 6V53T is the AIFV (page 76) and 300 L the V-150S (page 79).

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: The Commando V-150S and the Fire Support Vehicle each carry a secondary M60 7.62 mm machine gun. Which entry is correct?
options: Both 1,100 m maximum effective and 3,725 m maximum range; V-150S 800 rds/min, FSV 900 rds/min
Both 1,100 m maximum effective and 3,725 m maximum range; V-150S 900 rds/min, FSV 800 rds/min
Both 1,830 m maximum effective and 6,800 m maximum range; both fire 800 rds/min
V-150S 1,100 m maximum effective, FSV 1,700 m maximum effective; both fire 900 rds/min
explanation: Page 79 gives the V-150S M60 1,100 m effective, 3,725 m maximum and 900 rds/min. Page 81 gives the FSV M60 1,100 m, 3,725 m and 800 rds/min. The 1,830 and 6,800 m figures belong to the .50 cal M2.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which pair gives the COMBAT weights of the M113A2 APC and the AIFV?
explanation: Page 73 gives the M113A2 a combat weight of 11,070 kg (net 9,630 kg). Page 76 gives the AIFV 13,687 kg (net 11,373 kg).

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which data set matches the M113A2: forward speed, reverse speed, speed in water and fuel consumption?
options: 41 kph; 14.80 kph; 3 kph; 1.4 km per liter
66 kph; 14.80 kph; 6 mph; 4.1 km per liter
72 kph; 14.80 kph; 3 mph; 1.4 km per liter
66 kph; 14.80 kph; 3 mph; 1.4 km per liter
explanation: Page 73 gives forward 66 kph (41 mph), reverse 14.80 kph, in water 3 mph and 1.4 km per liter. The 72 kph figure belongs to the Sabrah and Guarani.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which dimensions match the M113A2: length, width, height and ground clearance?
explanation: Page 73 gives length 4.90 m, width 2.70 m, height 2.50 m and ground clearance 0.41 m. 6.14 m is the V-150S length (page 79) and 0.43 m is the Simba vertical obstacle (page 80).

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: What can the AIFV's 25 mm Oerlikon KBA do against aircraft, and how many rounds does the vehicle rack hold?
options: Brings down low flying aircraft at 1.5 km and attacks aircraft directly up to 2 km; 145 rounds
Brings down low flying aircraft at 2 km and attacks aircraft directly up to 1.5 km; 230 rounds
Brings down low flying aircraft at 2 km and attacks aircraft directly up to 1.5 km; 145 rounds
Brings down low flying aircraft at 3 km and attacks aircraft directly up to 2 km; 105 rounds
explanation: Page 76 says the KBA can bring down low flying aircraft at 2 km and attack aircraft directly up to 1.5 km, and the vehicle rack holds 145 rounds. 230 rounds are in the EWS and 105 is the HE authorization.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which comparison of road cruising range and combat weight is correct for the Simba and the Commando V-150S?
options: Simba 660 km and 10,160 kg; V-150S 644 km and 10,886 kg
Simba 644 km and 10,160 kg; V-150S 660 km and 10,886 kg
Simba 660 km and 10,886 kg; V-150S 644 km and 10,160 kg
Simba 482.80 km and 10,160 kg; V-150S 644 km and 11,070 kg
explanation: Page 80 gives the Simba a 660 km road range and 10,160 kg combat weight. Page 79 gives the V-150S 644 km and 10,886 kg.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which entry matches the fact sheet of the Sabrah Light Tank (ASCOD II)?
options: 105 mm 52-caliber coiled, low recoil gun; 8.368 m long; 8-V diesel compatible with NATO fuels
76 mm L23A1 gun; 8.368 m long; 8-V diesel compatible with NATO fuels
105 mm 52-caliber coiled, low recoil gun; 3.67 m long; Cummins ISC diesel compatible with NATO fuels
105 mm 52-caliber coiled, low recoil gun; 6.14 m long; Detroit Diesel 6V53 engine
explanation: Page 82 gives the Sabrah a 105 mm 52-caliber coiled, low recoil gun, a length of 8.368 m (height 3.67 m) and an 8-V turbo-charged diesel compatible with NATO fuels. The 76 mm L23A1 is the FSV gun (page 81).

prompt: A plan has squads assaulting the instant the AIFV ramps drop, allowing no time between halting and the assault. Which mechanized infantry limitation did the plan ignore?
options: AVs are restricted to certain avenues of approach
AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks
Infantrymen need sufficient time to mount and dismount
Dismounted infantrymen are vulnerable to small arms and indirect fire
explanation: Page 30 says infantrymen need sufficient time to mount and dismount. There was no enemy fire and the road was open, so the other limitations do not explain the delay.

prompt: A squad remounts its AIFV one at a time under cover, but inside, the soldiers keep rounds chambered with muzzles pointed up. Which SOP was violated?
options: Chamber empty, muzzle down
Provide cover while others are mounting
Once inside the AV, clear weapons and muzzle down
Move inside the AV one at a time
explanation: Page 45 (mounting SOPs) says once inside the AV, clear weapons and muzzle down. Chamber empty, muzzle down is the dismounting SOP (page 31); cover and one-at-a-time were followed.

prompt: Which two SOPs appear in BOTH the SOPs on dismounting and the SOPs on mounting?
options: Speed is of the essence; do not pile up at the door of the AV
Speed is of the essence; no riders on top of the AV
Chamber empty, muzzle down; move inside the AV one at a time
Provide cover while others mount; never hide behind an AV
explanation: Pages 31 and 45 both list that speed is of the essence and that soldiers must not pile up at the door of the AV. The other items belong to only one list.

prompt: A cavalry squadron on a long zone reconnaissance across open, dry plains must halt repeatedly because fuel, ammunition and spare parts cannot keep up. Which cavalry limitation does this show?
options: Mobility restricted by dense forest, steep terrain and water obstacles
Dependence on flatbeds for deployment to the theater
Mobility and firepower restricted in extremely close terrain
High logistics requirements
explanation: Page 61 lists high logistics requirements as a cavalry limitation. Terrain was not a factor, and flatbeds and close terrain are tank limitations (pages 67-68).

prompt: A planner orders a light tank platoon to lead a frontal push against enemy main battle tanks, assuming it can absorb the same fire. Which tank limitation was ignored?
options: Tanks are dependent on flatbeds for deployment to the combat theater
Mobility and firepower are restricted in extremely close terrain
Infantry units lack organic transport for the tanks' CSS needs
The light tank does not possess the level of protection of a main battle tank
explanation: Page 67 says the light tank does not possess the level of protection of a main battle tank.

prompt: A tank company occupies SBF positions on an open ridge with a surface danger zone and direct fire control measures planned. Enemy aircraft then attack. Which tank planning consideration was neglected?
options: Cover against enemy air
Surface danger zone
Direct fire control measures
SBF positions
explanation: Page 71 lists cover against enemy air as a tank planning consideration; the other three were planned.

prompt: A cavalry troop screens forward of its brigade at the planned distance from the main body, but no mortar or artillery unit is assigned to support it. Which cavalry planning consideration was neglected?
options: Indirect fire weapon support
Distance from main body
Security operations
Weapon range
explanation: Page 70 lists indirect fire weapon support first among the cavalry planning considerations; distance from the main body was planned.

prompt: Each of the four tanks in a tank platoon is crewed by a tank commander, a gunner and a driver. How many crewmen are in the platoon?
explanation: Page 65 shows four tanks, each with a commander, a gunner and a driver, or 12 crewmen. The platoon leader and platoon sergeant command two of the tanks.
